parole.significato: Forms adjectives.
parole.testo: From Latin past participles in -ītus, of verbs in -īre, -ĕre, -ēre, partly via Old French.

parole.significato: The act of annunciating.
parole.testo: From Middle English annunciacion, annunciation, from Latin annuntiātiō and Old French anonciacion.

parole.significato: A single-room dwelling for a hermit.
parole.testo: From Middle English celle, selle, from Old English cell (attested in inflected forms), from Latin cella (“chamber, small room, compartment”), later reinforced by Old French cel, sele, Old French cele. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *kelnā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelneh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱ

parole.significato: Self-assurance.
parole.testo: From Middle English confidence, from Latin cōnfīdentia (possibly via Old French confidence), from cōnfīdō (“believe, confide in”) from con- (“with”) + fīdō (“trust”). By surface analysis, confide + ence.

parole.significato: Small; diminutive.
parole.testo: From Middle English diminute, from Latin dīminūtus and Old French diminut.

parole.significato: Donor, one who donates.
parole.testo: From Middle English donatour, from Latin dōnātor and Old French; equivalent to donate + -or.

parole.significato: A proclamation of law or other authoritative command.
parole.testo: From Middle English edycte, borrowed from Latin edictum; earlier form edit, from Old French edit, from the same Latin word.

parole.significato: The full profits or products yielded by land, such as hay, pasturage, grain, rents, services, and the like.
parole.testo: From Latin expletia, Old French espleit. Compare exploit.

parole.significato: A band or cap (usually metal) placed around a shaft to reinforce it or to prevent splitting.
parole.testo: From Middle English verel, virel, virole (“ferrule; metal pivot on the end of an axle”), altered under the influence of Latin ferrum (“iron”), from Old French virole (“ferrule”), from Latin viriola (“little bracelet”), diminutive of viria (“bracelet worn by men”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *we

parole.significato: The physiological faculty of taste.
parole.testo: From Middle English gust, guste, from Latin gustus (“taste”) and Old French gust, goust.

parole.significato: Anything made of wool, or woolworking.
parole.testo: From Latin lanificium: compare Old French lanifice.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to praise, or the expression of praise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin laudatōrius: compare Old French laudatoire.

parole.significato: Slowness; sluggishness.
parole.testo: From Latin lentitūdo, from lentus (“slow”). Compare Old French lentitude.

parole.significato: The edge of the paper, typically left blank when printing but sometimes used for annotations etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English margyn, from Latin marginem (possibly via Old French margin), accusative of margō (“edge, brink, border, margin”). Doublet of marge and margo.

parole.significato: Mass; a church service.
parole.testo: From Middle English mes, partly from Old English mēse, mēose (“table”), a vernacular loan from Latin/Late Latin mē(n)sa (“table; meal”); and partly from Old French mes, Late Latin missum, from mittō (“to put, place (e.g. on the table)”). See mission, and compare Mass (“religious service”).

parole.significato: A dull or stupid person.
parole.testo: Ultimately from the name of Momus, god of mirth, through Latin and Old French.

parole.significato: The Church regarded as nourishing and protecting its members.
parole.testo: From an association of spiritual comfort and hierarchy with familial relationships, probably originally as a calque of similar expressions in other languages, especially 2nd-century Latin mater ecclesia (“mother church”) and 12th-century Old French mere eglise (“mother church”).

parole.significato: Any alteration or change.
parole.testo: Late 14th century as Middle English mutacioun, from Latin mūtātiō, both directly and via Old French mutacion.

parole.significato: Something which is packed, a parcel, a box, an envelope.
parole.testo: Equivalent to pack + -age. Possibly influenced by Anglo-Latin paccagium or Old French pacquage.

parole.significato: An entryway or gate.
parole.testo: Inherited from the Old English port, from the Latin porta (“passage, gate”), reinforced by the Old French porte. Doublet of porta.

parole.significato: Something prescribed; a rule, regulation or dictate.
parole.testo: Latin praescriptum: compare Old French prescript.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; Probably; modello unc/uncertain

parole.significato: Senses relating to placing or positioning.
parole.testo: From Middle English reposen (“to put (something) back, replace”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘again; back, backwards’) + posen (“to place (something)”), modelled after Latin repōnō (“to put back; to restore; to store”). parole.significato: residence; abode
parole.testo: Latin reseantia, Old French reseance.

parole.significato: Any of several Mediterranean herbs, of the genus Satureja, grown as culinary flavourings.
parole.testo: From Middle English saverey, possibly from Old English sæþerie, from Latin satureia, influenced by or via Old French savereie.

parole.significato: The north or northern regions.
parole.testo: From Middle English septentrion, septentrione, septemtryones, septemtrioun, from Latin septentriō, septentriōnem (“the northern regions, the north”) directly and through Old French septentrïon, septemtrion, from septentriōnēs (“the seven stars near the north pole”) (called Charles's Wain, or the Gre

parole.significato: A fine thin linen muslin or cambric cloth.
parole.testo: From Latin sindōn (possibly by way of Old French syndone and sindone), from Ancient Greek σινδών (sindṓn), from Late Egyptian šndy(t), from earlier šnḏwt (“kilt”).

parole.significato: Miscellaneous items or objects; (with possessive) personal effects.
parole.testo: From Middle English stuf, stuffe, from Anglo-Latin stuffa and its etymon Old French estofe, estoffe, estuf, estuffe, stoffe, from estoffer, estofer (“to provide what is necessary, equip, stuff”), borrowed from Old High German stoffōn, from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn (“to clog up, block, fill”). parole.significato: A specific pitch.
parole.testo: From Middle English ton, tone, from Latin tonus (“sound, tone”) (possibly through Old French ton), from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, “strain, tension, pitch”), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”). Doublet of tune, ton, tonos, and tonus.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or being a triumph.
parole.testo: From Middle English triumphal, triumphall, tryumphal, from Latin triumphālis and Old French trionfal, triumphal.

parole.significato: A word that indicates an action, event, or state of being.
parole.testo: From Middle English verbe, directly from Latin verbum (“word, verb”), reinforced by Old French verbe, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo-. Doublet of verve and word.
